questions.question: Unknown halide solutions: interpreting recorded silver-halide evidence
questions.subtopic: RP4 halide precipitate evidence and ionic equations
questions.prompt: Three hypothetical samples X, Y and Z each contain exactly one of chloride, bromide or iodide ions. A report records white precipitate for X, cream precipitate for Y and yellow precipitate for Z when silver ions were present. Reference data show the corresponding silver salts are AgCl (white), AgBr (cream) and AgI (yellow). (a) Assign each halide ion to X, Y and Z. (b) Write a balanced ionic precipitation equation for each. (c) Explain why the solid is electrically neutral even though the starting ions are charged. No laboratory procedure is required. [7 marks]
markPoints: X contains chloride ions, Cl⁻, because its precipitate is white.
Y contains bromide ions, Br⁻, because its precipitate is cream.
Z contains iodide ions, I⁻, because its precipitate is yellow.
Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) is the balanced chloride precipitation equation.
Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s) is the balanced bromide precipitation equation.
Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s) is the balanced iodide precipitation equation.
Each Ag⁺ ion combines with a halide ion of charge −1, giving a neutral formula unit AgX in the solid.
questions.modelAnswer: X contains chloride ions, Cl⁻, because its precipitate is white. Y contains bromide ions, Br⁻, because its precipitate is cream. Z contains iodide ions, I⁻, because its precipitate is yellow. Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) is the balanced chloride precipitation equation. Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s) is the balanced bromide precipitation equation. Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s) is the balanced iodide precipitation equation. Each Ag⁺ ion combines with a halide ion of charge −1, giving a neutral formula unit AgX in the solid.

questions.question: Four ion-test reports: carbonate, sulfate, ammonium and hydroxide
questions.subtopic: RP4 identifying carbonate sulfate ammonium and hydroxide ions
questions.prompt: Interpret four *already reported* classroom observations. Sample P produces a colourless gas that makes limewater cloudy in a reported acid reaction. Q is associated with a white insoluble barium sulfate precipitate. R releases a gas identified as ammonia from a reaction involving hydroxide ions. S is an aqueous solution with pH 12.5 and no other ions responsible for alkalinity. (a) Identify the diagnostic ion in each case: P carbonate, Q sulfate, R ammonium, S hydroxide. (b) Write three balanced net ionic equations for the observations about P, Q and R. (c) Explain how the pH data support the conclusion for S. Do not give methods for carrying out the tests. [8 marks]
markPoints: P contains carbonate ions, CO₃²⁻, since acid–carbonate reactions produce CO₂.
Q contains sulfate ions, SO₄²⁻, since the report identifies a BaSO₄ precipitate.
R contains ammonium ions, NH₄⁺, associated with the reported production of NH₃.
S contains hydroxide ions, OH⁻, accounting for an alkaline pH of 12.5.
The carbonate net ionic equation is CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O.
The sulfate precipitation net ionic equation is Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s).
The ammonium reaction net ionic equation is NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O.
Since pH 12.5 is greater than 7 at 25 °C, S is alkaline, consistent with dissolved hydroxide ions.
questions.modelAnswer: P contains carbonate ions, CO₃²⁻, since acid–carbonate reactions produce CO₂. Q contains sulfate ions, SO₄²⁻, since the report identifies a BaSO₄ precipitate. R contains ammonium ions, NH₄⁺, associated with the reported production of NH₃. S contains hydroxide ions, OH⁻, accounting for an alkaline pH of 12.5. The carbonate net ionic equation is CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O. The sulfate precipitation net ionic equation is Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s). The ammonium reaction net ionic equation is NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O. Since pH 12.5 is greater than 7 at 25 °C, S is alkaline, consistent with dissolved hydroxide ions.

questions.question: Three Group 2 metals: inferring trends from supplied solubility data
questions.subtopic: RP4 Group 2 hydroxide and sulfate solubility interpretation
questions.prompt: A written data table compares Mg, Ca and Ba compounds at 25 °C. Mg(OH)₂ is described as very slightly soluble, Ca(OH)₂ as sparingly soluble and Ba(OH)₂ as appreciably soluble; MgSO₄ is readily soluble, CaSO₄ less soluble and BaSO₄ very insoluble. (a) State how Group 2 hydroxide solubility changes down the group. (b) State the opposing trend for Group 2 sulfates. (c) Which listed hydroxide gives the highest concentration of OH⁻ in a saturated solution under these conditions, assuming no other chemistry? (d) Which listed sulfate would yield the largest persistent precipitate from equal available amounts? (e) Explain how the charges of Mg²⁺ and OH⁻ determine the Mg(OH)₂ formula and give its dissociation equation. (f) Identify why a single solubility observation does not establish an unknown metal's identity without reference comparisons. [7 marks]
markPoints: The hydroxides become more soluble down Group 2, from Mg(OH)₂ towards Ba(OH)₂.
The sulfates become less soluble down Group 2, from MgSO₄ towards BaSO₄.
Saturated Ba(OH)₂ provides the highest hydroxide ion concentration among the three stated solutions.
BaSO₄, being the least soluble listed sulfate, gives the most persistent solid for comparable amounts.
Mg²⁺ requires two OH⁻ ions for charge balance, giving formula Mg(OH)₂.
A formal dissolution equation is Mg(OH)₂(s) ⇌ Mg²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq), with the small solubility acknowledged.
A single solubility result is not unique identification: compare against standards and other evidence because several compounds can be partly soluble.
questions.modelAnswer: The hydroxides become more soluble down Group 2, from Mg(OH)₂ towards Ba(OH)₂. The sulfates become less soluble down Group 2, from MgSO₄ towards BaSO₄. Saturated Ba(OH)₂ provides the highest hydroxide ion concentration among the three stated solutions. BaSO₄, being the least soluble listed sulfate, gives the most persistent solid for comparable amounts. Mg²⁺ requires two OH⁻ ions for charge balance, giving formula Mg(OH)₂. A formal dissolution equation is Mg(OH)₂(s) ⇌ Mg²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq), with the small solubility acknowledged. A single solubility result is not unique identification: compare against standards and other evidence because several compounds can be partly soluble.

questions.question: Dehydration product: mass yield and distillation temperature evidence
questions.subtopic: RP5 distillation mass balance and boiling data
questions.prompt: This is a paper-only interpretation of reported data, not a preparation method. A theoretical reaction converts 0.250 mol of cyclohexanol into cyclohexene and water in a 1:1 mole ratio. The relative molecular mass of cyclohexene is 82.0 and 16.4 g of liquid product is recovered. Reference boiling points at the stated pressure are cyclohexene 83 °C and cyclohexanol 161 °C. A reported early distillate forms mainly at 82–84 °C; late fractions appear at 88–94 °C. (a) Calculate theoretical moles, maximum mass and percentage yield of cyclohexene. (b) Use the boiling points to explain what the early fractions suggest. (c) Explain why the broader, higher-temperature late fraction could contain impurities and why a boiling range by itself is not a definitive identity or purity test. [8 marks]
markPoints: The dehydration gives cyclohexene and cyclohexanol in a 1:1 mole ratio.
The theoretical maximum amount of cyclohexene is 0.250 mol.
The maximum mass is 0.250 × 82.0 = 20.5 g.
The percentage yield is 16.4/20.5 × 100 = 80.0%.
Cyclohexene has the lower reference boiling point, 83 °C, compared with cyclohexanol at 161 °C.
Early distillate collected at 82–84 °C is consistent with the more volatile cyclohexene.
Late fractions appearing over the higher, broader 88–94 °C range could contain impurities or a changing mixture.
A boiling range supports a provisional identification but cannot independently prove chemical identity or absolute purity.
questions.modelAnswer: The dehydration gives cyclohexene and cyclohexanol in a 1:1 mole ratio. The theoretical maximum amount of cyclohexene is 0.250 mol. The maximum mass is 0.250 × 82.0 = 20.5 g. The percentage yield is 16.4/20.5 × 100 = 80.0%. Cyclohexene has the lower reference boiling point, 83 °C, compared with cyclohexanol at 161 °C. Early distillate collected at 82–84 °C is consistent with the more volatile cyclohexene. Late fractions appearing over the higher, broader 88–94 °C range could contain impurities or a changing mixture. A boiling range supports a provisional identification but cannot independently prove chemical identity or absolute purity.

questions.question: Distillation and reflux: interpreting schematic apparatus descriptions
questions.subtopic: RP5 distillation versus reflux and boiling-point separation
questions.prompt: Two labelled apparatus sketches are described in words: in A, condensed vapour returns to the original reaction vessel; in B, condensed vapour is collected separately. Reference boiling points for hypothetical liquid pairs are Pair 1 at 83 °C and 161 °C; Pair 2 at 78 °C and 82 °C. (a) Name the process represented by A and B. (b) Explain their different purposes. (c) Explain why a fractional separation may distinguish Pair 2 better than a simple distillation, and why Pair 1 is easier to separate. (d) State the physical function of a condenser, without giving any experimental set-up instructions. [7 marks]
markPoints: Sketch A represents heating under reflux, because condensed vapour returns to the original vessel.
Sketch B represents distillation, because condensed vapour is collected separately.
Reflux helps a reaction proceed without continually losing volatile material from the vessel.
Distillation separates and recovers more volatile components or product from a mixture.
Pair 2 differs in boiling point by only 4 °C and is hard to separate cleanly by simple distillation.
Fractional distillation provides repeated evaporation–condensation enrichment; Pair 1 has a much larger 78 °C boiling-point difference and is easier to separate.
A condenser changes vapour into liquid by cooling it; its purpose is not to chemically change the product.
questions.modelAnswer: Sketch A represents heating under reflux, because condensed vapour returns to the original vessel. Sketch B represents distillation, because condensed vapour is collected separately. Reflux helps a reaction proceed without continually losing volatile material from the vessel. Distillation separates and recovers more volatile components or product from a mixture. Pair 2 differs in boiling point by only 4 °C and is hard to separate cleanly by simple distillation. Fractional distillation provides repeated evaporation–condensation enrichment; Pair 1 has a much larger 78 °C boiling-point difference and is easier to separate. A condenser changes vapour into liquid by cooling it; its purpose is not to chemically change the product.

questions.question: Distillation fractions: recovery, losses and mixture inference
questions.subtopic: RP5 fraction mass balance and purity limitations
questions.prompt: A paper-only table reports a 25.0 g starting liquid mixture that contains 15.0 g of a target compound whose reference boiling point is 72 °C. A collector's report lists an early 12.0 g fraction at 70–73 °C, an intermediate 4.0 g fraction at 76–85 °C and a late 8.0 g fraction at 107–111 °C. A second component has reference boiling point 109 °C. (a) Find total collected mass and the mass not recovered. (b) Calculate recovery of target mass if the early fraction is assumed to consist entirely of target. (c) Relate early and late temperature bands to the reference boiling points. (d) Explain the likely significance of the intermediate wide fraction. (e) Give one reason why the computed recovery is only an estimate rather than proof that all 12.0 g is pure target. [8 marks]
markPoints: The three recorded fractions total 12.0 + 4.0 + 8.0 = 24.0 g.
The uncollected mass is 25.0 − 24.0 = 1.0 g.
Assuming all 12.0 g early fraction is target, recovery = recovered target/initial target × 100.
Calculated target recovery is 12.0/15.0 × 100 = 80.0%.
The early temperature range 70–73 °C agrees approximately with the target's 72 °C reference boiling point.
The late 107–111 °C range agrees approximately with the second component's 109 °C reference boiling point.
The intermediate 76–85 °C range could contain a transition mixture rather than a single pure component.
Mass and boiling temperature alone cannot establish the early fraction's full purity, so the 80% estimate assumes pure target in that fraction.
questions.modelAnswer: The three recorded fractions total 12.0 + 4.0 + 8.0 = 24.0 g. The uncollected mass is 25.0 − 24.0 = 1.0 g. Assuming all 12.0 g early fraction is target, recovery = recovered target/initial target × 100. Calculated target recovery is 12.0/15.0 × 100 = 80.0%. The early temperature range 70–73 °C agrees approximately with the target's 72 °C reference boiling point. The late 107–111 °C range agrees approximately with the second component's 109 °C reference boiling point. The intermediate 76–85 °C range could contain a transition mixture rather than a single pure component. Mass and boiling temperature alone cannot establish the early fraction's full purity, so the 80% estimate assumes pure target in that fraction.

questions.question: Four unknown compounds: identifying functional groups from test results
questions.subtopic: RP6 unknown functional groups from reported observations
questions.prompt: A worksheet reports four independent results for one pure compound in each sample. A causes the orange colour of bromine water to disappear. B gives a silver deposit with Tollens' reagent. C produces a gas confirmed as carbon dioxide in a reaction with carbonate. D changes acidified dichromate(VI) from orange to green but gives no positive Tollens' test. Assume the listed samples belong only to the following classes: alkene, aldehyde, carboxylic acid, or primary/secondary alcohol. (a) Identify the most likely functional group for A–D and justify each from the given observations. (b) Explain the key type of change behind A's result and behind B's result. (c) State why D's two observations cannot alone distinguish a primary from a secondary alcohol. This is interpretation of supplied evidence, not an instruction to perform tests. [8 marks]
markPoints: A is an alkene because bromine water is decolourised by reaction at a C=C double bond.
B is an aldehyde because it gives the characteristic silver deposit in Tollens' test.
C is a carboxylic acid because acid plus carbonate releases carbon dioxide.
D is an oxidisable primary or secondary alcohol, given the orange-to-green oxidation reagent and negative Tollens' result within the stated options.
The alkene undergoes addition across its carbon–carbon double bond in the reaction associated with A.
For B, silver(I) ions are reduced to metallic silver while the aldehyde is oxidised.
Oxidation of dichromate(VI) reagent to Cr³⁺ accounts for the orange-to-green observation with D.
Both primary and secondary alcohols can show oxidation, so the dichromate result and a negative Tollens' test alone do not distinguish which class D belongs to.
questions.modelAnswer: A is an alkene because bromine water is decolourised by reaction at a C=C double bond. B is an aldehyde because it gives the characteristic silver deposit in Tollens' test. C is a carboxylic acid because acid plus carbonate releases carbon dioxide. D is an oxidisable primary or secondary alcohol, given the orange-to-green oxidation reagent and negative Tollens' result within the stated options. The alkene undergoes addition across its carbon–carbon double bond in the reaction associated with A. For B, silver(I) ions are reduced to metallic silver while the aldehyde is oxidised. Oxidation of dichromate(VI) reagent to Cr³⁺ accounts for the orange-to-green observation with D. Both primary and secondary alcohols can show oxidation, so the dichromate result and a negative Tollens' test alone do not distinguish which class D belongs to.

questions.question: Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols: interpreting product identities
questions.subtopic: RP6 oxidation product evidence and classifying alcohols
questions.prompt: Three hypothetical alcohols are known structural isomers with molecular formula C₄H₁₀O. Given reports say: P yields butanal (which gives a positive Tollens' observation) after oxidation; Q yields butanone (which does not); R is not oxidised in the same mild conditions. The possible identities are butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. (a) Match P–R with the alcohol structures and classify each alcohol as primary, secondary or tertiary. (b) State the carbonyl class from P and Q. (c) Give a general balanced oxidation equation using [O] for a primary alcohol yielding an aldehyde. (d) Explain why R does not readily oxidise without breaking a carbon–carbon bond. [8 marks]
markPoints: P is butan-1-ol, the primary alcohol in the list.
Q is butan-2-ol, the secondary alcohol in the list.
R is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, the tertiary alcohol in the list.
The oxidation product butanal from P is an aldehyde.
The oxidation product butanone from Q is a ketone.
Primary-alcohol oxidation to an aldehyde can be written RCH₂OH + [O] → RCHO + H₂O.
Secondary alcohol oxidation can form a ketone, whereas tertiary alcohol R is not readily oxidised in the same mild conditions.
A tertiary alcohol's carbon bearing –OH has no directly bonded hydrogen, so ordinary oxidation would require breaking a carbon–carbon bond.
questions.modelAnswer: P is butan-1-ol, the primary alcohol in the list. Q is butan-2-ol, the secondary alcohol in the list. R is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, the tertiary alcohol in the list. The oxidation product butanal from P is an aldehyde. The oxidation product butanone from Q is a ketone. Primary-alcohol oxidation to an aldehyde can be written RCH₂OH + [O] → RCHO + H₂O. Secondary alcohol oxidation can form a ketone, whereas tertiary alcohol R is not readily oxidised in the same mild conditions. A tertiary alcohol's carbon bearing –OH has no directly bonded hydrogen, so ordinary oxidation would require breaking a carbon–carbon bond.

questions.question: Three organic formulas: what functional-group evidence can and cannot prove
questions.subtopic: RP6 molecular formula versus functional-group identity and isomerism
questions.prompt: A set of *already recorded* organic observations is supplied. U has molecular formula C₄H₈O and gives a positive Tollens' result. V has formula C₃H₆O₂ and produces carbon dioxide in a reported carbonate reaction. W has formula C₄H₈ and decolourises bromine water. For this question assume each is a simple acyclic molecule with one main functional group and that competing side reactions are absent. (a) Identify the most strongly supported functional group for U, V and W. (b) Give two distinct structural isomer names consistent with U and explain why the single positive result cannot distinguish them. (c) Name one likely identity for V and explain how its result distinguishes the acid from an ester with the same formula. (d) Give one alkene name consistent with W and say why W is not uniquely identified from this test. [8 marks]
markPoints: U contains an aldehyde group because it gives the characteristic positive Tollens' observation.
Butanal is a C₄H₈O structural isomer consistent with U.
2-Methylpropanal is another C₄H₈O structural isomer consistent with U.
A positive Tollens' result distinguishes aldehydes from ordinary ketones, but cannot distinguish the two proposed aldehyde skeletons.
V contains a carboxylic acid group because the reported carbonate reaction releases CO₂.
Propanoic acid fits C₃H₆O₂; an isomeric ester would not normally give this characteristic acid–carbonate gas test.
W contains an alkene C=C group because bromine water is decolourised in the stated simple-molecule context.
But-1-ene is one possible C₄H₈ alkene, but but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene are alternatives so the colour-change alone is not unique structural identification.

Butanal is a C₄H₈O structural isomer consistent with U. 2-Methylpropanal is another C₄H₈O structural isomer consistent with U. A positive Tollens' result distinguishes aldehydes from ordinary ketones, but cannot distinguish the two proposed aldehyde skeletons. V contains a carboxylic acid group because the reported carbonate reaction releases CO₂. Propanoic acid fits C₃H₆O₂; an isomeric ester would not normally give this characteristic acid–carbonate gas test. W contains an alkene C=C group because bromine water is decolourised in the stated simple-molecule context. But-1-ene is one possible C₄H₈ alkene, but but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene are alternatives so the colour-change alone is not unique structural identification.
